After showering Cheongpung with praise without pausing for breath, Jeok Cheongang pointed at him again.
“Watch carefully how he dodges.
Now, when I send a finger flick...”
*Whoosh!
Thud!*
The finger flick struck Cheongpung squarely in the temple, and his eyes flew open.
He looked around through eyes still heavy with sleep, then rubbed his head when the pain finally seemed to register.
“Ow.
That hurts...”
Then he returned to dreamland faster than light.
I stared at Jeok Cheongang.
“Clear as a mirror?
What?”
“A clear mirror...
Forget it.
You and that brat both.
To hell with all of it!”
The Yangtze was peaceful today, too.

chapters.title: Chapter 442
paragraphs: Like the majestic waters of the Yangtze, time flowed slowly but steadily onward.
It was late afternoon on the fourth day since we had left Sichuan by Murim reckoning. As I sat on the deck, a familiar presence approached.
“What are you doing?”
I knew who it was just from his footsteps.
Without taking my eyes off the Yangtze, I answered, “What does it look like I’m doing?”
Hyuk Mujin limped over and answered without hesitation.
“Looks like you’re just sitting there.”
“I’m thinking.”
“About what?”
“The peace of Murim.”
After a brief silence, hearty laughter burst out.
“Puhaha! That’s the funniest joke I’ve heard all year. That’s our Captain.”
“No. Forget it. I just thought of something else.”
“What?”

“There’s a certain bastard who always takes everything I say for dog shit. But maybe because he’s been feeling better lately, he doesn’t seem able to control his mouth. So I’m wondering whether I should beat him a few times. What do you think?”
Hyuk Mujin considered the question for a moment.
“It isn’t the person I’m thinking of, is it?”
“Probably.”
“Who is it?”
“Someone named Hyuk Mujin.”
“Be quiet unless you want another taste of the Yangtze.”
Hyuk Mujin nodded frantically, practically having a seizure.
“Please, anything but that...!”
A few days earlier, I had sentenced him to a Yangtze dunking and immediately logged out, leaving him to spend an entire shichen sightseeing at the Yangtze Aquarium.

The moment Mungyeong’s superb medical skills had restored him to reasonable health, he had even cast a fishing line, declaring that he would catch every last bastard that had bitten his nose and slice them into sashimi.
“Fine, calm down. Why are you here?”
“Huh?”
“I’m asking what you want. There must be a reason.”
Hyuk Mujin asked in a wounded voice, “Do I really need a reason to come see you? Between us?”
“If you don’t have one, you get a taste of the Yangtze.”
“I have one! I do!”
“Then spit it out.”
“This might just be me, but...”
Hyuk Mujin hesitated before continuing.
“Is something bothering you lately?”
“Why?”
“No reason. It’s just that whenever I look at you these days, you seem to have a lot on your mind.”
“Me?”
“Yes. And, well... To be honest, not much has happened lately compared to before. But somehow, you’re the only one who seems tired and busy. I guess that’s the best way to put it.”
“You seem to be sleeping more often, too.”
When had this bastard gotten so perceptive?
Under my strange gaze, Hyuk Mujin scratched the back of his head.
“Well, that’s just the impression I got. Am I wrong?”
“Yeah. You are.”
Naturally, my answer was a lie. Hyuk Mujin’s guess was exactly right.
Since first setting foot in Murim, I had never traveled between the two worlds as often as I had lately.
*Looking back, though, every one of those trips was my own choice.*
Sometimes a Quest had blocked the Logout function, but most of the time, I had made the decision myself.
If I had crossed over to the other world and spent time there while walking across thin ice, my tension would have collapsed, and I would have been unable to overcome the crisis.
But recently, the situation had changed.
*Both the modern world and Murim have made it over a mountain.*
How long had it been since both worlds had fallen quiet at the same time?
Murim had been a minefield of constant upheaval from the very beginning. Even the relatively peaceful modern world had started growing turbulent after my conflict with Lee Jungryong.
For the first time in ages—no, for the first time since I had obtained the System—I had found peace in both worlds.
But deep down, I had a suspicion bordering on certainty.
This peace would not last long.
The calm before the storm. The brief peace I had been given was like the stillness of the night before a storm broke.

That was why I was busily traveling between the two worlds, preparing for the storm soon to come. It was also why, even with the breathtaking scenery of the Yangtze spread out before me, I was still hunched over a mystery that refused to yield.
*What the hell is this?*
I stared at the paper in my hand.
The not particularly high-quality xuan paper was covered with strange patterns and symbols I had drawn myself.
There were all kinds of them, each subtly different in shape. They looked like some mysterious script out of a detective novel.
No. I almost wished that were all they were. Then I wouldn’t have to worry so much.
“What’s that?”
“A storm.”
“Huh?”
“Honestly, I don’t really know either.”
Or perhaps I already knew and simply didn’t want to believe it.
These patterns and symbols were the sole point of overlap between two worlds with different flows of time, different histories, and different cultures.
In the modern world, they had been found in the Arch Lich’s magic circle. In Murim, they had appeared in Dark Heaven’s formations.
And now, deep in my heart, I was turning over a single word.
*Black magic.*
I had no idea how bizarre or far-ranging Murim’s demonic, heterodox arts—commonly called demonic martial arts—could be.
But the more I looked back on everything I had personally seen and experienced, the more it resembled black magic.
*The Blood Lord. The Western Heaven Demon Lord. Even the formation we found in the cave.*

The Blood Lord’s recovery after being struck by Jeok Cheongang’s Dance of the Fire God and Demon had resembled a Troll’s regeneration more than anything human. The Lord of Heaven, whom the Western Heaven Demon Lord worshiped so fervently, had appeared before me through the body of a subordinate who was already dead.

On top of that, the formations used by the black-robed men who had followed their respective leaders and drenched Shaolin and Sichuan in blood were astonishingly similar to what the modern world called Warp Gates.
*At this point, it would be stranger not to suspect anything.*
At the same time... the fact that I did not want to believe it easily was my reality.
Black magic in Murim.
This was more serious than having a female friend I secretly had a crush on use the bathroom at my house, only to find the toilet seat left up afterward.
*Where did it come from? How? Why?*
My head was full of question marks. An investigation was already underway in the modern world, but I felt as though I were wandering through endless fog.
More frightening still was the unknown something lurking beyond that fog, yet to reveal itself.
If all my fears turned out to be true, then...
“What are you staring at so intently?”
The voice shattered my deep thoughts and brought me back to reality. I frowned.
Not because my train of thought had been interrupted, but because of the rancid stench assaulting my nose.
Suppressing an instinctive gag, I asked, “You haven’t washed again, have you?”
Gung Gibang, who had subtly pressed his butt against the spot beside me, nodded.
“It’s only natural for a beggar not to wash. Is there a problem?”
Hyuk Mujin opened his mouth with a queasy expression.
“Young Hero Gung, are you some kind of poison man? The moment you came within three jang, my head started spinning and I began dry-heaving.”
“A Beggars’ Sect disciple washes only three times in his life: when he is born, when he joins the Beggars’ Sect, and when he dies.”
I turned to Gung Gibang, who was spouting this bullshit.
“Then go dunk yourself in the river before I kill you right now. Since you’re going in anyway, scrub off some of that grime while you’re at it.”
“No. I hate water. Especially after that day.”
Ah. Right. He was another victim of the Yangtze dunking.
Gung Gibang answered with a grave expression, then glanced at the paper in my hand.
“Were you looking at that again?”
“Again? Young Hero Gung, you knew about it?”
At Hyuk Mujin’s question, Gung Gibang nodded.
“Of course. A few days ago, he suddenly told me to follow him and showed it to me. Asked if I’d ever seen it anywhere before. Naturally, I told him I’d never seen anything like it in my life.”
“Captain, how could you discriminate against me like this?”
I gave the wounded Hyuk Mujin a warm smile.
“Easily.”
“I showed it to him because he’s the Successor Beggar. I thought he might know something. Satisfied?”
Having found something to tease Hyuk Mujin about, Gung Gibang snickered.
“He showed it to Mungyeong, too.”
“Hey, that was...”
I opened my mouth, but I couldn’t exactly reveal Mungyeong’s identity, so I closed it again.
It wasn’t only because Mungyeong was watching us from several jang away while pointedly stroking a large acupuncture needle.
*Seriously.*
“See that, you Hyuk bastard? That’s where you stand. Not in his heart, but in his little toe—urk!”
*Grab. Whoosh!*
Listening to him was getting so irritating that my ears hurt. I grabbed Gung Gibang by the collar and hurled him over the railing.
He flailed in midair, then plunged into the river with a short scream.
*Splash!*
He must have struck the water fairly hard, because the spray reached the ship’s railing.
The next moment, Cheongpung, who had been giggling at the surprise entertainment, suddenly screamed.
“No! Mimi!”
What now?
I peered more closely to see what had happened, then doubted my eyes.
A horned snake, pure white from head to tail, was thrashing wildly as it swam toward us for dear life.
The clear waters of the Yangtze were turning pitch-black around Gung Gibang, while several fish that had been swimming peacefully nearby floated belly-up.
“...What the fuck?”
Even the Thousand-Year Poison Horned Snake was reacting like that. Had Hyuk Mujin been right? Was Gung Gibang really some kind of poison man?
The river bandits who witnessed this absurd case of water pollution unfold in real time began seriously debating whether Gung Gibang belonged to the Beggars’ Sect or the Sichuan Tang Clan.
I let out a deep sigh and gestured to them.
“Get him out quickly. If you want to keep working as river bandits on the Yangtze.”
Realizing that their home waters were under threat, the river bandits sprang into action.
After that, I continued traveling between the modern world and Murim once or several times a day, handling everything I needed to do while continuing my investigation.
News that my Peace Guild and the Wizard Guild led by Magic Johnson had entered into some kind of agreement became a major topic of conversation among Hunters around the world.
But for ordinary people, the bigger story was still me—the individual named Jin Taekyung.

World Hunter Association: “Jin Taekyung is an undeniable S-rank Hunter and a hero who has saved countless lives. The fact that he is still classified as an A-rank Hunter is absurd.” He is expected to visit the Association headquarters for a brief test, after which he will be issued an S-rank Hunter license. The World Hunter Association sends Jin Taekyung a fervent invitation!
Breaking News: Jin Taekyung flatly rejects the Association’s offer. “Circumstances make it difficult for me to go right now. I’ll stop by when I have time.” World Hunter Association left bewildered.
World Hunter Association issues new statement: “This is unprecedented. S-rank Hunter testing and licensing have always been conducted at Association headquarters.”
Jin Taekyung: “I didn’t say I wouldn’t take the test. I said I’d go later. I can take it in Korea, so what’s the problem? Instead of arguing about precedent, let’s try being efficient.”
A senior Hunter Association official, wounded in his pride, issues a threat: “Then we cannot issue you an S-rank Hunter license.”

Urgent Breaking News: Brief social-media post reads, “Then don’t. Who the hell do you think you are, threatening me? Fucking hell.” Account confirmed to be Jin Taekyung’s official social-media account... Public reaction? “That was unbelievably satisfying.” “More refreshing than the soda we drank during the Thousand-Ri March.”

World Hunter Association: “The official’s statement was a personal slip and does not represent the organization’s position. We apologize.” Final decision made to dispatch a testing team to Korea for Jin Taekyung.
Japanese Prime Minister Koizumi: “Jin Taekyung is fun, cool, and sexy. I will make certain that he becomes a naturalized Japanese citizen. Because that is my ‘promise’...”
Leaving behind the countless incidents and remarks surrounding me, I returned to Murim.
And then...
“I can finally breathe again. Damn Yangtze.”
With Jeok Cheongang’s refreshing remark ringing out, the bow of the swift ship finally entered Hubei Province after nearly ten days of sailing.

chapters.title: Chapter 443
paragraphs: Ten days of sailing had been anything but easy.

We weren’t aboard some massive cruise ship. We’d been stuck on a wooden vessel, shuttling between musty cabins and damp decks. Ports? Our schedule was so tight that we’d kept our eyes ahead and sailed straight on.
Under the circumstances, even Jeok Cheongang—and the river bandits who called the Yangtze their home turf—brightened.
Of course, one person was happier than all the rest.
“Ohhh, finally...”
Mu Song, who had been forced to volunteer his talents all the way to Hubei Province, trembled with emotion.
He had been sunk in grief ever since one of his swift ships sank, but now, as if he had forgotten every hardship he’d suffered along the way, he shouted in a powerful voice.
“Drop anchor! Hurry up so we can leave this damn...!”
Jeok Cheongang, who had been nodding in satisfaction, turned toward him.
“This damn what?”
Mu Song realized he had let his true feelings slip and shook his head at tremendous speed.
“N-no, sir. I meant the Yangtze.”
“Of course you meant the Yangtze. That’s what this old man meant, too.”
“Unless you were calling *us* damnable?”
“W-why would I ever do that?”
It certainly looked like he would.
While Mu Song broke out in a cold sweat beneath Jeok Cheongang’s narrowed gaze, the river bandits sensed their leader’s peril and sprang into action.
The swift ships gradually slowed, lined up along the pier, and dropped anchor. A murmur rose from the people gathered near the harbor.
“That flag...”
“The Yangtze River Channel League. It’s the Yangtze River Channel League!”
“What does it say underneath? Water Dragon Stronghold? Never heard of it.”
“It’s a river stronghold based in Sichuan. Water Dragon Stronghold is led by Ship-Fire Boy Mu Song, the Seafaring King’s second Disciple.”
“Now that you mention it, I think I’ve heard of them. But why are those bastards in Hubei when they’re supposed to be in Sichuan?”
“How should I know? Damn river bandits. Things have been tense enough lately as it is...”
“Shh. Keep your voice down. Some young man is looking this way. Nothing good comes from getting tangled up with Murim.”
The group of merchants who met my eyes hurried away.
And they weren’t the only ones.
A fisherman whose face had been blackened by the sun grabbed his net and scurried off, while a vendor selling his catch packed up his stall at the speed of light.
In the distance, an official in formal robes watched us closely, surrounded by an escort of government troops.
Their eyes held undisguised wariness.
*What the hell? This atmosphere is completely different from Sichuan.*
The Yangtze River Channel League might have been a band of river pirates founded on plunder, but it had rules and an established system of its own.

I’d heard they didn’t simply pounce whenever they spotted an opportunity, kill everyone in sight, and strip the ship bare. Sometimes they even protected vessels from unaffiliated river bandits, and under normal circumstances, they only collected a set toll before letting ships pass.
*They tested the waters during the Great Faction War, but in the end, they sided with the orthodox faction.*
Give and take made the world go round.
During the upheaval that decided the future of Murim, the Yangtze River Channel League had backed the orthodox faction and slipped the government enough bribes to keep it satisfied.
In other words, they were hired thugs in a cloak of legality, tolerated by both sides and allowed to carry on.

They couldn’t exactly be called good people, but this was Murim, where every kind of lunatic imaginable ran wild. They might not be gentlemen, but by Murim standards, they were at least run-of-the-mill scoundrels.
*That’s why ordinary people in Sichuan barely reacted to them.*
Their attitude had been more like, *Those beggar bastards are still alive and back again?* They certainly hadn’t openly avoided us like this.
I tilted my head as I watched the people scatter in every direction.
*Is it just a difference in atmosphere from one region to another?*
But if that were all, Mu Song’s expression wouldn’t have looked so grim.
He stared at the suddenly deserted harbor with a deep frown, then called over his right-hand man.
“Have we received no word from our brothers in the League?”
“No, Stronghold Lord. They must have known we were coming, but for some reason, there has been no contact.”
“Not even from Dangyang Stronghold or Honghu Stronghold?”
“That is correct.”
“Even if the others didn’t know, Uncle Hwang is at Donghu Stronghold. There’s no way he failed to hear that we were coming...”
Mu Song muttered with a grave expression, then continued.
“Once we disembark, send out our fastest men to find out what’s happening. Contact our nearby brothers immediately as well.”
“Yes, Stronghold Lord.”
At Mu Song’s gesture, the river bandits under his command moved as one. We were no exception, having finished our preparations to disembark long ago.
Jeok Cheongang, finally leaving the Yangtze behind, led the way. I followed, then Jin Wikyung, Cheongpung, Hyuk Mujin, and Gung Gibang.
Mungyeong came too, blending so quietly into the crowd that one could almost forget he was there.
At last, Jeok Cheongang—the Fire Pokémon finally free of his type disadvantage—wore a radiant smile.
“Whew. I can finally breathe again. This is why people are meant to live with their feet on solid ground.”
But his happiness didn’t last long.
“You there. Stop.”
The voice was filled with authority. An official who had approached without us noticing swallowed nervously as he looked at us.
Then he glanced at the hundreds of government troops behind him, puffed out his chest, and continued.
“I hear you came from Sichuan. Is that correct?”
“‘You’? ‘Is that correct’?”
Jeok Cheongang blinked and echoed the official’s words back at him.
“Were you addressing this old man just now?”
“That is correct.”
“‘That is correct’?”
The official’s eyes wavered uneasily. But he quickly steeled himself and raised his voice.
“Ahem! Answer only what this official asks. State clearly where you came from and what purpose brings you here!”
“‘Ahem’? ‘Answer me’? ‘State your purpose’?”
“N-no, this old man...”
“‘Old man’?”
*Don’t. Don’t do it. Please, just stop.*
They said women got butterflies when a handsome man repeated someone’s words like that, but from where I stood, this was a horror movie.
I hurriedly stepped in before Jeok Cheongang could drive a Flame God Palm into the arrogant official’s chest.
“Talk to me instead.”
“I have nothing to discuss with some wet-behind-the-ears brat!”
I’d just pulled him out of a tiger’s jaws, and this was how he talked to me?
I wanted to knock his head clean off, but I held back and continued.
“We did come from Sichuan, and we have business here.”
“Then what business would that be?”
“Well...”
At that moment, someone shouted excitedly.
“Steamed fish topped with lots of minced chili peppers!”
“Cheongpung, you son of a bitch!”
“Why, Benefactor? It really is delicious. It’s so good that if two people were eating it and one dropped dead, the other wouldn’t even notice...”
I didn’t know if it was really delicious enough that one person could die without the other noticing, but from the official’s expression, it was clear that we looked like people who deserved to die.
His face turned bright red as he bellowed.
“How dare you mock this official!”
“Wait, mister. That’s not what he meant...”

“It is suspicious enough that you came from Sichuan under the flag of the Yangtze River Channel League, and now you claim you came here to eat steamed fish? You’re the sort who won’t shed a tear until you see the coffin. Guards, arrest them at once!”
“Yes, sir!”
*What the hell was this development?*
Before I could say another word, hundreds of government troops with military discipline drilled into them surrounded us with spears. Jin Wikyung clicked his tongue softly and stepped forward.
“You’re rather quick-tempered.”
Jin Wikyung was tall even by modern standards. In Murim, he was considered a giant.
The official swallowed hard as he took in Jin Wikyung’s Ural Mountain shoulders and the muscles bulging beneath his clothes.
“W-who are you?”
“I am Jin Wikyung of the Jin Family of Taiyuan in Shanxi. I won’t waste words, so why don’t you withdraw your men?”
Before the official could answer, Jin Wikyung continued in his deep voice.
“It seems you haven’t been informed yet, but we are martial artists who received direct permission to pass from the City Lord of Sichuan Province.”
“The City Lord of Sichuan Province?”
“If you doubt me, you may verify it. But before you do, I suggest you withdraw your men. There’s no need to throw away perfectly good lives.”
The official flinched, and the spearpoints of the government troops surrounding us trembled.
They knew it too. No matter how rigorous their training or how elite they were, they couldn’t defeat us.
But that was how the world worked. The men at the bottom shed the blood, while the men at the top guarded their pride. I saw the official’s eyes harden.
“How dare you... Do you even know who this official is?”
Without the slightest change in expression, Jin Wikyung replied.

“I do. Naturally, you belong to the Hubei Provincial Administration Commission, which oversees the province’s civil and financial affairs. Judging by your robes, you are a Judicial Inquirer of the secondary sixth rank. Though I don’t know why a man responsible for judicial affairs has come all the way out here to arrest innocent people.”
“Oh, that reminds me. Do you know a man surnamed Yi, with the given name Hongcheon?”
A trembling voice slipped between the official’s lips.
“T-that person is the Provincial Administration Commissioner who was newly appointed not long ago.”

“I see. I thought I’d heard something about that. From Assistant Provincial Administrator in Shanxi to Provincial Administration Commissioner of Hubei. Quite the promotion. An occasion worth celebrating.”
“M-might I ask what your relationship is with the Provincial Administration Commissioner?”
Jin Wikyung smiled faintly. At some point, his posture and tone had naturally shifted into those of a man looking down at the official.
“I’ve met him a few times and shared a drink or two with him. I also helped him when he needed it.”
“Gasp!”
“Why? Is there something else you’d like to hear?”
“N-no, sir!”
The official’s rigid back folded like a mollusk.
After snapping into a deep bow toward Jin Wikyung, he spun around and roared at his subordinates.
“You fools! What are you doing? Put away those vicious blades at once!”
“Y-yes, sir!”
“What sort of idiots can’t even read a situation like this? Please forgive our rudeness!”
Jin Wikyung benevolently patted the official on the shoulder.
“It’s all right. Everyone makes mistakes in life, like you did today.”
“This man Son is deeply moved by your generosity, as vast as the sea!”
“Don’t apologize to me. Apologize to these men directly. Especially the gentleman you addressed first. He is a highly respected elder of Murim.”
“I-I had no idea. Then might I ask his sobriquet...?”
“He is Great Hero Jeok Cheongang, the Fire King.”
“We came straight to Hubei after the Sichuan Blood Tragedy, aboard a ship borrowed from the Yangtze River Channel League. Oh, and of course, we didn’t come solely to eat steamed fish.”
*Stop it. You’re going to make him cry.*
The official looked from one of us to another with an expression that said he wanted to die, performing the remarkable feat of bowing five times a second.
Jin Wikyung nudged me lightly in the ribs.
“What do you think, my youngest? Your big brother looks cool, doesn’t he?”
“You would’ve looked cool if you hadn’t said that.”
“Once you establish connections with the government, they make many things more convenient. If you ever find yourself in trouble, try using my name.”
If he could say that with such confidence, he must have planted quite a few seeds.
According to Gung Gibang, the Jin Family of Taiyuan’s meteoric rise in such a short time was virtually unprecedented.

If Jin Mukyung, who was undoubtedly continuing his grueling training at the Jin Family even now, was a martial arts genius, then Jin Wikyung was an all-rounder who possessed everything a Family Head needed.
“My youngest, don’t you think I look cool? Hm?”
Yes. Apart from things like this, he was the perfect Family Head.
I was still trying to push away the increasingly clingy Jin Wikyung when it happened.
“Everyone, stand aside.”
At the voice infused with profound internal energy, the people murmuring some distance from the harbor parted to either side.
At the same time, dozens of martial artists carrying considerable qi approached us with measured steps.
*That’s...*
I narrowed my eyes.
Written in cloud-like calligraphy across their pure-white silk martial robes were the words:
**Zhuge Clan.**

paragraphs: The Zhuge Clan.
It was a famous family bound to appear at least once in every modern wuxia novel.
Not a single character with the surname Zhuge was ever stupid, and none of them were conspicuously strong, either.
They were supposedly one of Murim’s great families, yet martial arts seemed more like their minor than their major.
That made sense. The Zhuge Clan’s true strength came not from their bodies, but from their minds.
They were a family of wise men versed in a broad range of scholarship, strategy, and mechanisms and formations.
As a result, the world called them the Divine Mechanism Zhuge, and in Murim, they handled practically every role that required brains.
If the strategist of the Murim Alliance in a novel you were reading didn’t have a name that began with Zhuge, it almost felt wrong.
Perhaps that image of the Zhuge Clan had been lodged so firmly in my mind that seeing these martial artists stride toward us without hesitation felt strangely unfamiliar.
But unfamiliarity wasn’t the only emotion I felt.
Clack-clack-clack-clack!
The Zhuge Clan’s martial artists lined up on either side of the road like iron towers. A lone figure slowly walked between them.
The slender young man wore robes so white they were almost blinding.
“The stars shone unusually bright last night. It seems they were heralding the arrival of honored guests. I am the Zhuge Clan’s Lesser Family Head...”
Delighted, I thrust a hand into the air and shouted.
“Galgyun!”
“Not ‘Galgyun’... My name is Zhuge Gyun.”
A heavy silence fell.
The Zhuge Clan’s martial artists, who still had no idea who I was, looked at me as if I were some kind of madman. Jeok Cheongang looked at me with a hint of confusion.
“You know this fellow?”
“Yes. I met him at the Star-Array Grand Banquet last time. But this is the first I’ve heard that he’s the Zhuge Clan’s Lesser Family Head.”
“Even someone like you has friends?”
“He’s not my friend. I just call them the Three Idiots...”
“Ahem! Ahem-ahem!”
One of the Three Idiots I had met at the Star-Array Grand Banquet—the Divine Marvel Dragon Zhuge Gyun—hurriedly cleared his throat and cut me off.
Before I could say anything, he turned toward Jeok Cheongang and offered his greetings.
“Zhuge Gyun, a newcomer to Murim, pays his respects to Senior.”
Jeok Cheongang looked Zhuge Gyun up and down, then tossed out a question.
“What relation are you to Gonghu?”
“Pardon?”
“I mean the Fan-Wisdom King, Zhuge Gonghu. The bastard who served as the Murim Alliance’s chief strategist during the Great Faction War.”
I had heard both the title and the name of the Fan-Wisdom King Zhuge Gonghu.
He had served as the mind of the Murim Alliance during the Great Faction War and had been the foremost contributor to turning around the grim course of the war.
That was one reason he had been hailed as one of the Ten Kings alongside the other Supreme Peak masters.
*And he calls a man like that a bastard.*
I had seen Jeok Cheongang act this way so many times that I was used to it, but to everyone else, it must have been a whole new world.
Jin Wikyung swallowed hard, while the Zhuge Clan’s martial artists stood with their mouths hanging open, doubting their own ears.
Of course, our Fire King Jeok Cheongang didn’t care about any of that. Ramming straight into things with blazing force was practically the Fire Gate Clan’s trademark.
“Well? Why aren’t you answering?”
His expression was unpleasant enough already, but when he actually frowned, he looked like a murderous demon.
Even Zhuge Gyun—a lunatic who was no slouch himself—was so flustered that he stammered.
“M-my great-grandfather.”
“Is that so? No wonder you look a little like him. You look like you’ve got a decent head on your shoulders. Like you’ve got no manners, either.”
Now that was imposing.

Since Jeok Cheongang was a man from two generations ago who had lived well past a hundred, even the elders of most prestigious clans and sects couldn’t dare object when he called them, “Hey,” “you,” or “bastard.”
He chewed people up with martial arts and digested them with seniority. He was Murim’s very own Bodhidharma skull water.
As the atmosphere grew increasingly awkward, I gave Jeok Cheongang a light poke in the side.
“Come on. That’s enough.”
“What? Can’t this old man say even that much?”
“Even so, he passed away ten years ago...”
“What do these greenhorns know? If this old man had died, Zhuge Gonghu would have done the same. He and I have been calling each other bastard for years.”
Not brotherly terms. Bastardly terms.
While everyone flinched once again at his innovative choice of words, Jin Wikyung was the first to recover and address Zhuge Gyun.
“Thank you for the Zhuge Clan’s hospitality.”

A true professional was a true professional. At the Star-Array Grand Banquet, Zhuge Gyun had seemed like a man with a screw loose, but as the Lesser Family Head of his clan, he responded appropriately.
“Think nothing of it. I hope your journey here was not too uncomfortable.”
“If a person is comfortable in both body and mind, how can he call himself a martial artist—”
“It was damn uncomfortable. How dare you make this old man come all the way here? I’ll hear the reason, and if it’s nothing important, then a Flame Divine Palm will...”
“Oh, seriously! I said that’s enough!”
“You dare grab this old man’s sleeve! Let go, you all-brawn bastard!”
While I tried to restrain Jeok Cheongang, who had suddenly flown off the handle, Jin Wikyung hurriedly continued.
“I know this is rude, but let’s put the pointless conversation aside and hurry. Please, let’s hurry.”
“A wise decision. Zhuge Wuhou, who laid the foundations of our family, would have slapped his feather fan down and agreed.”

The government troops and Zhuge Clan martial artists were the first to clear a path at the dramatic show of unity between the two Lesser Family Heads. The river bandits from the Water Dragon Stronghold who had joined our party followed behind them.
As we moved, I felt countless wary gazes following us and heard the whispers all around.
*What the hell is going on?*
Was this why Jin Wikyung had said we needed to pass through Hubei?
I didn’t have long to wonder. The moment we climbed into the carriage, Mungyeong quietly spoke.
“It seems we’re one person short.”
“What?”
I looked around and only then noticed that someone was missing.
“Wait. Where did he go?”
“Over here, Benefactor!”
When the hell had that bastard gotten over there?
Cheongpung was standing in front of a street stall that had not yet been folded, stuffing himself with freshly steamed fish. He raised one hand high and shouted.
“I’ll finish eating and come!”
“Stop talking bullshit and get your ass over here!”
Please.
Just for one day, let’s live like human beings. Like human beings.
With my heart in tatters, the carriage began to move.
Even as it raced down the well-kept road and disappeared into the distance, the people’s gazes clung to us like shadows.

Unlike Emei, Qingcheng, and the Tang Clan—the prestigious powers of Sichuan Province—which had established their bases on mountains or in remote areas, the Zhuge Clan occupied the heart of a broad thoroughfare.
Just the people passing outside the carriage window numbered well over several hundred.
Their faces were deeply tanned, and whenever they spotted the carriage bearing the Zhuge Clan’s emblem, they bowed their heads.
“Why are there so many people here?”
Zhuge Gyun, who sat across from me, answered my mutter.
“The Yangtze is Hubei’s lifeline. It makes the vast surrounding lands fertile, so people naturally gather here. And since every year brings a plentiful harvest, smiles never leave their faces.”
“Really? The people I saw at the ferry about one shichen ago looked like their smiles had left forever.”
“That...”
Zhuge Gyun fell silent and looked away, wearing a grave expression that didn’t suit him.
“I’ll tell you after we reach the family compound.”
Something must have happened. At the Star-Array Grand Banquet, he had been an endless fountain of nonsense, so it was telling that even he looked like this now.
Given the mood, I didn’t press him and turned toward the window.
*Something definitely feels wrong.*
And the more time passed, the more that suspicion deepened.
The government troops, who were usually so lax, had their eyes wide open as they checked people’s hopae at various points, while martial artists in ordinary clothes hid among the commoners.
The martial prowess I briefly sensed from them as we passed was far from low. Dark Heaven immediately came to mind, but Jeok Cheongang’s Sound Transmission cleared up the matter a moment later.
*—They’re Zhuge Clan people. For some reason, they’re hiding their identities and even moving covertly.*
*They’re going this far in what’s practically their own front yard?*
I suddenly remembered what had happened a few days earlier and asked,
*—Old Master, didn’t you hear anything?*
*—About what?*
*—You know. You left with my eldest brother for a while last time.*
*—I did.*
*—Didn’t you hear why we had to come to Hubei then? Something about Wudang or the Zhuge Clan?*
Jeok Cheongang’s brow furrowed slightly as he looked at me.
*—What good would it do this old man to hear any of that?*
*—Pardon?*
*—If we’re going, we’re going. Why bother prying into every last detail? I merely badgered him to get here as quickly as possible. I told him I’d sink every one of the swift ships if he didn’t.*
*—...Ah. Right.*
I wasn’t sure whether to call that cool or hotheaded.
Shaking my head, I glanced at Mungyeong.
The boy had been chatting with Hyuk Mujin with a bright smile, showing no sign of irritation. But then one of his eyebrows lifted slightly.
A private Sound Transmission reached my ears.
*—What.*
*—...I haven’t even said anything yet.*
*—Don’t stare at me for no reason. Not if you want to see the sun rise tomorrow.*
How was I supposed to breathe with him scaring me like this?
I sighed inwardly and turned my gaze beyond the carriage’s latticed window.
Mount Longzhong, also called Mount Fulong because the greatest strategist under heaven—a man who had shaped the history of an era—had once lived there in seclusion.
And spread across a vast stretch of land, the Zhuge Clan finally came into view.
*They said this was the wealthiest family in Hubei Province.*
Their ancestor, Zhuge Kongming, had been renowned for his frugality. But his descendants had not devoted their naturally sharp minds solely to scholarship, mechanisms, and formations.
They had taken full advantage of the fertile land that yielded plentiful harvests every year and the Yangtze’s waterways, which crossed the entirety of Hubei Province, to amass enormous wealth.
I began to grasp the extent of that wealth before we even passed through the Zhuge Clan’s main gate.
“Why aren’t we getting out? Haven’t we arrived?”
Zhuge Gyun answered with an expression that seemed to say he had no idea what I was talking about.
“Pardon? It would take quite a while to walk from here to the Inner Hall. We still have seven more gates to pass through, so just remain seated.”
“...It’s that big?”
“This is after we reduced it. Our family suffered considerable damage during the Great Faction War.”
“That’s insane. You’re raking in gold and silver. Didn’t your ancestor leave instructions telling you to live frugally or something? Wasn’t he supposed to be an incorruptible scholar?”
Without the slightest change in expression, Zhuge Gyun answered in a solemn voice.
“Studying isn’t cheap. Do you know how expensive books are? Besides, our family also provides separate support to scholars.”
“You need a comfortable environment to pass the civil-service examinations and advance in martial arts. When you’re hungry, you can’t think about anything. You only become anxious.”
“Uh... right.”
It wasn’t what I had expected, but when I thought about it, every one of his points made sense.
After patiently explaining the importance of capital, Zhuge Gyun concluded his speech by saying that even his ancestor, Zhuge Kongming, had been born with a silver spoon in his mouth.
By then, the carriage had passed through all eight gates and was entering the Inner Hall.
“Now, please get down and follow me. The Family Head is waiting.”
“The Family Head would be...”
“My father.”
I had heard about him from Jeok Cheongang.

During the Great Faction War, Zhuge Gonghu had lost his only son. In accordance with the principle of eldest-son succession, he had bestowed the position of Lesser Family Head upon his young grandson.
That young grandson was Zhuge Feng, the Crouching Dragon Guest—the current Family Head of the Zhuge Clan and Zhuge Gyun’s father.
“Family Head, I’ve brought the honored guests.”
At Zhuge Gyun’s grave voice, now completely devoid of humor, the firmly closed doors slowly opened.

sentences.text: The Zhuge Clan.
It was a famous family bound to appear at least once in every modern wuxia novel.
Not a single character with the surname Zhuge was ever stupid, and none of them were conspicuously strong, either.
They were supposedly one of Murim’s great families, yet martial arts seemed more like their minor than their major.
That made sense.
The Zhuge Clan’s true strength came not from their bodies, but from their minds.
They were a family of wise men versed in a broad range of scholarship, strategy, and mechanisms and formations.
As a result, the world called them the Divine Mechanism Zhuge, and in Murim, they handled practically every role that required brains.
If the strategist of the Murim Alliance in a novel you were reading didn’t have a name that began with Zhuge, it almost felt wrong.
Perhaps that image of the Zhuge Clan had been lodged so firmly in my mind that seeing these martial artists stride toward us without hesitation felt strangely unfamiliar.
But unfamiliarity wasn’t the only emotion I felt.
Clack-clack-clack-clack!
The Zhuge Clan’s martial artists lined up on either side of the road like iron towers.
A lone figure slowly walked between them.
The slender young man wore robes so white they were almost blinding.
“The stars shone unusually bright last night.
It seems they were heralding the arrival of honored guests.
I am the Zhuge Clan’s Lesser Family Head...”
Delighted, I thrust a hand into the air and shouted.
“Galgyun!”
“Not ‘Galgyun’...
My name is Zhuge Gyun.”
A heavy silence fell.
The Zhuge Clan’s martial artists, who still had no idea who I was, looked at me as if I were some kind of madman.
Jeok Cheongang looked at me with a hint of confusion.
“You know this fellow?”
“Yes.
I met him at the Star-Array Grand Banquet last time.
But this is the first I’ve heard that he’s the Zhuge Clan’s Lesser Family Head.”
“Even someone like you has friends?”
“He’s not my friend.
I just call them the Three Idiots...”
“Ahem!
Ahem-ahem!”
One of the Three Idiots I had met at the Star-Array Grand Banquet—the Divine Marvel Dragon Zhuge Gyun—hurriedly cleared his throat and cut me off.
Before I could say anything, he turned toward Jeok Cheongang and offered his greetings.
“Zhuge Gyun, a newcomer to Murim, pays his respects to Senior.”
Jeok Cheongang looked Zhuge Gyun up and down, then tossed out a question.
“What relation are you to Gonghu?”
“Pardon?”
“I mean the Fan-Wisdom King, Zhuge Gonghu.
The bastard who served as the Murim Alliance’s chief strategist during the Great Faction War.”
I had heard both the title and the name of the Fan-Wisdom King Zhuge Gonghu.
He had served as the mind of the Murim Alliance during the Great Faction War and had been the foremost contributor to turning around the grim course of the war.
That was one reason he had been hailed as one of the Ten Kings alongside the other Supreme Peak masters.
*And he calls a man like that a bastard.*
I had seen Jeok Cheongang act this way so many times that I was used to it, but to everyone else, it must have been a whole new world.
Jin Wikyung swallowed hard, while the Zhuge Clan’s martial artists stood with their mouths hanging open, doubting their own ears.
Of course, our Fire King Jeok Cheongang didn’t care about any of that.
Ramming straight into things with blazing force was practically the Fire Gate Clan’s trademark.
“Well?
Why aren’t you answering?”
His expression was unpleasant enough already, but when he actually frowned, he looked like a murderous demon.
Even Zhuge Gyun—a lunatic who was no slouch himself—was so flustered that he stammered.
“M-my great-grandfather.”
“Is that so?
No wonder you look a little like him.
You look like you’ve got a decent head on your shoulders.
Like you’ve got no manners, either.”
Now that was imposing.

Since Jeok Cheongang was a man from two generations ago who had lived well past a hundred, even the elders of most prestigious clans and sects couldn’t dare object when he called them, “Hey,” “you,” or “bastard.”
He chewed people up with martial arts and digested them with seniority.
He was Murim’s very own Bodhidharma skull water.
As the atmosphere grew increasingly awkward, I gave Jeok Cheongang a light poke in the side.
“Come on.
That’s enough.”
“What?
Can’t this old man say even that much?”
“Even so, he passed away ten years ago...”
“What do these greenhorns know?
If this old man had died, Zhuge Gonghu would have done the same.
He and I have been calling each other bastard for years.”
Not brotherly terms.
Bastardly terms.
While everyone flinched once again at his innovative choice of words, Jin Wikyung was the first to recover and address Zhuge Gyun.
“Thank you for the Zhuge Clan’s hospitality.”
A true professional was a true professional.
At the Star-Array Grand Banquet, Zhuge Gyun had seemed like a man with a screw loose, but as the Lesser Family Head of his clan, he responded appropriately.
“Think nothing of it.
I hope your journey here was not too uncomfortable.”
“If a person is comfortable in both body and mind, how can he call himself a martial artist—”
“It was damn uncomfortable.
How dare you make this old man come all the way here?
I’ll hear the reason, and if it’s nothing important, then a Flame Divine Palm will...”
“Oh, seriously!
I said that’s enough!”
“You dare grab this old man’s sleeve!
Let go, you all-brawn bastard!”
While I tried to restrain Jeok Cheongang, who had suddenly flown off the handle, Jin Wikyung hurriedly continued.
“I know this is rude, but let’s put the pointless conversation aside and hurry.
Please, let’s hurry.”
“A wise decision.
Zhuge Wuhou, who laid the foundations of our family, would have slapped his feather fan down and agreed.”
The government troops and Zhuge Clan martial artists were the first to clear a path at the dramatic show of unity between the two Lesser Family Heads.
The river bandits from the Water Dragon Stronghold who had joined our party followed behind them.
As we moved, I felt countless wary gazes following us and heard the whispers all around.
*What the hell is going on?*
Was this why Jin Wikyung had said we needed to pass through Hubei?
I didn’t have long to wonder.
The moment we climbed into the carriage, Mungyeong quietly spoke.
“It seems we’re one person short.”
“What?”
I looked around and only then noticed that someone was missing.
“Wait.
Where did he go?”
“Over here, Benefactor!”
When the hell had that bastard gotten over there?
Cheongpung was standing in front of a street stall that had not yet been folded, stuffing himself with freshly steamed fish.
He raised one hand high and shouted.
“I’ll finish eating and come!”
“Stop talking bullshit and get your ass over here!”
Please.
Just for one day, let’s live like human beings.
Like human beings.
With my heart in tatters, the carriage began to move.
Even as it raced down the well-kept road and disappeared into the distance, the people’s gazes clung to us like shadows.

Unlike Emei, Qingcheng, and the Tang Clan—the prestigious powers of Sichuan Province—which had established their bases on mountains or in remote areas, the Zhuge Clan occupied the heart of a broad thoroughfare.
Just the people passing outside the carriage window numbered well over several hundred.
Their faces were deeply tanned, and whenever they spotted the carriage bearing the Zhuge Clan’s emblem, they bowed their heads.

Zhuge Gyun, who sat across from me, answered my mutter.

chapters.title: Chapter 445
paragraphs: Clack.
“Ah.”
Someone let out a small gasp.
The enormous library revealed when the doors opened was impressive enough, but so was the fact that they had opened without anyone touching them or using internal energy.
Even to someone who had spent his entire modern life passing through automatic doors tens of thousands of times, it was a remarkably novel experience.
*Some kind of machine?*
*No, this was Murim. Should I call it a mechanism?*
The doors contained an intricate arrangement of iron and wooden components, all precisely interlocked.
And that wasn’t all. As I slowly looked around the library, I saw unmistakable traces of similar mechanisms throughout the place.
Of course, they were crude compared to the cutting edge of modern civilization. But I had certainly never seen anything like them in any of the other prestigious great families or sects I’d visited.
*That aside...*
*Why is nobody here?*
There wasn’t even a servant or guard in sight, let alone the Family Head himself.
As everyone, myself included, stared around, Zhuge Gyun shouted.
“Family Head!”
His voice, infused with internal energy, echoed through the library.
The space wasn’t merely large. Vast was the only word for it. It was bigger than a modern soccer stadium.
Zhuge Gyun’s shout carried between the endless rows of bookshelves, but no answer came.
“What the hell? Is he not here?”
“He seems to be somewhere inside, but... Ah, this is driving me crazy.”
As if he had known this would happen, Zhuge Gyun let out a deep sigh and continued.
“He often gets like this when he becomes absorbed in something. I’m sorry, but if you could wait here for a moment, I’ll find the Family Head and—”
Jeok Cheongang, who had been looking around the library, cut him off.
“Enough. Is that really necessary?”
“Pardon? Even so, with Great Hero Jeok visiting...”
“He’ll come out when the time is right. He must have his reasons.”
For a moment, I wondered if I had heard him correctly. Of all people, I never expected those words to come from Jeok Cheongang.
Even Cheongpung dropped the candied fruit he had been bringing to his mouth.
*Am I dreaming?*
I was seriously considering the question when Jeok Cheongang continued with a warm smile.
“Come to think of it, this old man has never seen such a large and magnificent library in his life. Would it be all right if I looked around for a while?”
Zhuge Gyun answered with a dazed expression.
“Of course.”
“Even if I burn it down?”
“...Pardon?”
“It was a joke, you little punk. Ho-ho. How could I burn everything in sight when I’m here as a guest?”
Jeok Cheongang laughed heartily, then added,
“Knocking over a bookshelf by accident would be another matter.”
In the next instant, Jeok Cheongang shot upward like a streak of light.
At the same time, a palm strike carrying the tremendous force of ten thousand geun slammed into the nearest bookshelf.
Boom!
It happened before anyone could stop him. I stared at the scene unfolding before me, my mouth hanging open.
*Oh, fuck.*
Rumble...
The bookshelf, which looked to be at least three zhang tall, began to tilt.
And there were hundreds of them.
In the blink of an eye, the countless shelves packed together at regular intervals became one enormous row of dominoes.
“W-wait, wait, wait, wait!”
Crash! Rumble-rumble-rumble!
The deafening roar swallowed Zhuge Gyun’s scream.
As every bookshelf came crashing down, years of accumulated dust erupted into the air and filled the library in a dense cloud.
No, I wasn’t even sure it could still be called a library. A graveyard of books would have been more appropriate.
It might even have become one person’s grave.
“Fatherrrr!”
Jeok Cheongang patted the wailing Zhuge Gyun on the shoulder.
“You’re the new Family Head of the Zhuge Clan now.”
“Nooo!”
Whack!
Jeok Cheongang smacked him on the back of the head and gave him an incredulous look.
“You really can’t take a joke, can you? Can’t you see your father over there, alive and well?”
Jeok Cheongang was telling the truth.
A couple of coughs came from within the thick cloud of dust, and a slender figure emerged, waving one hand as he walked toward us.
“Well, now. Cough. I’m sorry I couldn’t come out to greet you sooner. There have been an unusual number of matters requiring my attention lately. Cough.”
“At least you know. What an ill-mannered brat.”
Jeok Cheongang answered curtly and flicked his sleeve.
Whoosh!
Compressed air burst outward, scattering the dust cloud. At last, the man came fully into view.
“Ha. Seeing you like this makes me realize how much time has passed. Do you remember this old man?”
A clear voice answered.

“Of course. It was the fifth Mid-Autumn Festival after my birth. Senior ate two plates of roast duck and drank five jars of Yeoahong, then fought a duel with Great Hero Peng as the gathering drew to a close and ended up with a bloody nose.”
“What? That Thunderbolt Saber King bastard was there too? We even fought?”
“Yes. Great Hero Peng laughed loudly and struck the table, spilling wine on Senior’s knee. It was a minor disagreement.”
“That sounds like a major incident where it wouldn’t have been strange for someone to die.”
Jeok Cheongang let out a quiet laugh before continuing.
“Quite a few years have passed, but that incredible head of yours is still as sharp as ever. All right, enough nonsense. Come here. You have guests waiting for you.”
“I was planning to greet them regardless.”
Though the middle-aged man was covered in dust, it couldn’t conceal his refined appearance.
He was the youngest Sect Leader of any prestigious great family or sect I had met so far. His eyes, unusually clear and radiant, turned toward us.
“My apologies for keeping such honored guests waiting. I am Zhuge Feng.”
It was a remarkably plain greeting for the Family Head of the Zhuge Clan, the foremost great family in Hubei Province and one of the central pillars of the orthodox faction.
Then, before anyone could respond, Zhuge Feng continued. The moment I heard his next words, I suddenly understood why his sobriquet was Crouching Dragon Guest.

“Time is as precious as gold, and I have no desire to take anyone else’s gold. Only those who wish to remain need stay. Oh, and I’ve always believed people should make themselves comfortable when they talk, so please don’t take this the wrong way.”
I wondered what he meant until Zhuge Feng promptly flopped onto his side, paying no attention to the dust coating the floor. A laugh escaped me.
“Sure, why not? This is comfortable.”
I lay down at an angle and propped my chin on one hand. The corners of his eyes curved like crescent moons.
Though everyone looked dumbfounded, they sat down one by one and listened to Zhuge Feng.
Mu Song tried to leave, saying he had to visit a Yangtze River Channel League stronghold in Hubei, but one remark from Zhuge Feng stopped him in his tracks.
“I won’t stop you if you wish to leave, but what I am about to say concerns you deeply as well, Ship-Fire Boy Mu Song.”
Mu Song hesitated, then remained behind. Surprisingly, Mungyeong, who had seemed the most likely to leave first, stayed quietly where he was.
Then again, with everyone else remaining, leaving alone might have drawn even more attention.

The Zhuge Clan’s intelligence network had already informed Zhuge Feng that this young medical apprentice was the Divine Physician’s Disciple. He gave Mungyeong a curious look, but soon turned away and began to speak.
“It was exactly one month ago. I was in the library, reading the *Records of the Grand Historian* for the eighty-fifth time, when I heard the news.”
The Nine Sects and One Gang and the Five Great Families were the leading powers of their respective provinces.
With roots stretching back anywhere from a hundred years to several centuries, each possessed a dense intelligence network that allowed them to know their territory like the palm of their hand.
The Zhuge Clan was no exception.
“The Sea Serpent Society had disappeared.”
“The Sea Serpent Society? What’s that, Benefactor?”
“I don’t know either.”
Unlike the bewildered Cheongpung and me, everyone else’s eyes widened.
Mu Song’s reaction stood out more than anyone else’s.
“Th-the Sea Serpent Society?”
“Yes, the very one you know. The association formed by the countless fishermen and boatmen of Hubei Province.”
Ah. Now I understood.
I had never heard of the Sea Serpent Society, but I could guess what kind of organization it was.
To put it simply and dispense with all the old-fashioned explanations, it was a sort of professional association.
Just as each region had a Hunter Association, Hubei Province had—or rather, used to have—an association of fishermen called the Sea Serpent Society.
And this was unquestionably good news, at least for Mu Song. The faint smile tugging at the corners of his mouth was proof enough.
“I cannot say what the Zhuge Clan thinks of this, but as someone devoted to the League, I welcome the news. The Sea Serpent Society caused my Master no end of trouble.”
“I thought you would feel that way. At least within Hubei Province, it was the only organization capable of standing against the Yangtze River Channel League.”
Tributaries of the Yangtze ran throughout Hubei Province like a spiderweb.
No matter how powerful the Yangtze River Channel League was, it must have been vastly outnumbered by the people who made their living from fishing.
Though Hubei was outside the Sichuan territory under his responsibility, Mu Song laughed heartily at the news that one powerful rival had disappeared.
“But how did they end up disbanding? Did they happen to smuggle salt or something...?”
Zhuge Feng shook his head.

“Of course not. Even if they had been smuggling salt, the Sea Serpent Society would never have handled it so carelessly. And if they had been caught, a fleet dispatched by order of the Son of Heaven would already be filling the Yangtze throughout Hubei.”
“Then was it an internal conflict?”
“I don’t think you properly understood what I said.”
His clear, transparent eyes fixed on Mu Song.
As he faced Mu Song’s confusion, Zhuge Feng continued slowly.
“The Sea Serpent Society disappeared. Someone crushed it utterly.”

“The night before I received that report, a banquet was held to celebrate the Society Head’s eightieth birthday. Forty-five shipowners who had sworn loyalty to him and roughly a thousand members of the Sea Serpent Society attended. They drank until past midnight and launched dozens of pleasure boats onto the waters of Red Cliffs. And that was the last of it.”
The next morning, an old boatman who rose at dawn found the waters of Red Cliffs choked with corpses and the wreckage of brutally shattered boats.
The Society Head and the organization’s core members, including dozens of shipowners, had all met their deaths at Red Cliffs. The Sea Serpent Society had lost both its head and its body.
Nothing can move without either.
The Sea Serpent Society, which had stood shoulder to shoulder with the Yangtze River Channel League and wielded power throughout Hubei Province for decades, disappeared just like that.
“H-how could such a thing happen...?”
“It is strange that you, of all people, knew nothing about it.”
Zhuge Feng stared steadily at the speechless Mu Song.

“Do you know who moved first after the incident at Red Cliffs became known? The authorities? The Sea Serpent Society members who were lucky enough to survive? No. It was the Yangtze River Channel League. They invaded the Sea Serpent Society’s territory and took control of the Yangtze with astonishing speed.”
“...Great Hero Zhuge.”
Mu Song’s face hardened.
Like the rest of us, he seemed to have finally realized why he had needed to remain.
“Are you saying you suspect me? The League?”
“Of course I didn’t. The Great Hero Hwang of Donghu Stronghold whom I know is not such a foolish man. He is different from the other foolish, violent Stronghold Lords.”
Zhuge Feng brushed the dust from his shoulder and smiled faintly at Mu Song.
“That was certainly what I thought—until the Dongting Fisherman, who had publicly condemned the Yangtze River Channel League, disappeared three days ago.”
At that moment, unrest spread through the group, and a familiar notification rang in my ears.
Ding.
